This action is said to be irreducible if M does not leave invariant any definable non-trivial proper subgroup of S. Prove that if S is a simple group such that every proper definable subgroup of S is nilpotent, and the action of M on S is irreducible, then this action is equivalent to the action of S on itself by conjugation.
Prove that a simple group of finite Morley rank without involutions cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a connected group other than on itself acting by conjugation.

Prove that a simple(that is, without proper non-trivial connected normal subgroups) algebraic group M over an algebraically closed field cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a simple group of finite Morley rank other than M/Z(M).

Is the(standard, restricted) wreath product G ≀ H of two finitely generated Hopfian groups Hopfian? The same question where G is assumed to be abelian or nilpotent is equivalent to Kaplansky’s direct finiteness conjecture; see(H. Bradford, F. Fournier-Facio, Math. Z., 308, no. 4(2024), Paper no. 58).

A graph is called a cograph if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a path with 4 vertices. A graph is said to be chordal if it has no induced cycles with n vertices for every n ⩾ 4. For a finite group G, the enhanced power graph E(G) is the graph with vertex set G and edges {x, y} for all x ̸= y ∈ G such that ⟨x, y⟩ is cyclic. (a) For a given integer n ⩾ 4, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) has no induced cycles with n vertices. (b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) is chordal. In(Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18073) we proved that if the enhanced power graph of a given finite group is a cograph, then it is also chordal. Also the finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph is a cograph are described, and additional information is obtained on finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph has no induced cycles with 4 vertices.

For a finite group G, the power graph P(G) is the graph with vertex set G and edges {x, y} for all x ̸= y ∈ G such that either x ∈ ⟨y⟩ or y ∈ ⟨x⟩. Is it true that, for every finite group G, if P(G) is a cograph, then P(G) is chordal? Cf. 21.23. This holds if every element of G has prime power order(D. Bubboloni, F. Fumagalli, C. E. Praeger, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18073) and if G is a nonabelian simple group(J. Cameron, P. Manna, R. Mehatari, J. Algebra, 591(2022), 59–74; J. Brachter, E. Kaja, J. Algebr. Comb., 58(2023), 1095–1124).

(T. Breuer, R. M. Guralnick). Let G be a finite simple group and let p1, p2 be any(not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of |G|. Then can we always find Sylow pi-subgroups Hi such that G = ⟨H1, H2 ⟩?

(F. Lisi, L. Sabatini). Let G be a non-trivial finite group and let p1,..., pk be the distinct prime divisors of |G|. For each i, let Hi be a Sylow pi-subgroup of G. Is it true that there exists an element x ∈ G such that for all i the subgroup Hi ∩ Hix is inclusion-minimal in {Hi ∩ Hig: g ∈ G}?

(M. Larsen, A. Shalev, P. H. Tiep). A permutation on a set Ω is called a derangement if it has no fixed points in Ω. Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group. Is it true that every element in G is the product of two derangements?

Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group, and let δ(G) be the proportion of derangements in G. Is it true that δ(G) ⩾ 89/325? Note that δ(G) = 89/325 for the action of the Tits group G = 2 F4(2)′ on the cosets of a maximal parabolic subgroup of the form 22.[28 ].S3(Forum Math. Sigma, 13(2025), paper no. e98, 62 pp.).

Let G ⩽ Sym(Ω) be a finite primitive permutation group with a regular suborbit(that is, G has a trivial 2-point stabiliser). Then is it true that for all α, β ∈ Ω, there exists γ ∈ Ω such that the 2-point stabilisers Gα,γ and Gβ,γ are both trivial?

(Well-known question). A discrete group G is said to have the Haagerup property(also known as Gromov’s a-T-menability property) if there exists a metrically proper isometric action of G on a(possibly infinite-dimensional) Hilbert space. Are all 1-relator groups Haagerup groups?
Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.
Is the following problem decidable, and if so, what is its complexity? Given a finite group G, is there a finite group H such that the derived subgroup of H is isomorphic to G?

Does an analogue of Dunwoody’s theorem hold for totally disconnected locally compact groups, that is, must a tdlc group of rational discrete cohomological dimension at most 1 be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?

(Well-known problem). A group G is a unique product group if, for any nonempty finite subsets A, B of G, there exists an element of G which can be written uniquely as ab with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. A group G is locally invariant orderable if G admits a partial order < such that for all g, h ∈ G with h ̸= 1, we have either gh > g or gh−1 > g. Does there exist a unique product group which is not locally invariant orderable?

Let G be a finite group, w a multilinear commutator group-word, and p a prime. Suppose that p divides the order |xy| whenever x is a w-value of p′-order in G and y is a w-value in G of order divisible by p. Is it true that then the verbal subgroup w(G) must be p-nilpotent? Without the assumption that w be multilinear, the answer is negative. An affirmative answer has been obtained in several special cases(J. Algebra, 609(2022), 926–936). Y. Contreras Rojas,

Kropholler’s hierarchy(see 15.45) is closed under finite extensions, that is, (Hα F)F ⊆ Hα F for every α (P. Kropholler, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 90(1993), 55–67). Let a hierarchy of tdlc groups HK be defined analogously to Kropholler’s hierarchy in 15.45, with K being the class of profinite groups and with the cell stabilisers of the admissible action required to be open. Is it true that HK is closed under profinite extensions, that is, (Hα K)K ⊆ Hα K for every α?

By definition, a constructible totally disconnected, locally compact(tdlc) group is the result of a sequence of profinite extensions and ascending HNN-extensions starting from the trivial group. As in the discrete case, soluble constructible tdlc groups have type F P∞ (G. C. Cook, I. Castellano, J. Algebra, 543(2020), 54–97). Are soluble tdlc groups of type F P∞ constructible?

(S. Harper, C. Donoven). The spread of a group G is the greatest nonnegative integer k such that for all nontrivial elements x1,..., xk ∈ G there exists y ∈ G such that ⟨x1, y⟩ = · · · = ⟨xk, y⟩ = G, or is ∞ in case there is no such maximum. Does there exist a group with spread equal to 1? Such a group must be infinite if it exists(T. C. Burness, R. M. Guralnick, S. Harper, Ann. Math., 193(2021), 619–687).

It is known that there exist residually finite, locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms(A. B. Apps, J. Algebra, 81(1983), 320–339). Are there any locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms that are not residually finite?
Let G be a subgroup of GL(n, Q) with finitely many orbits under automorphisms. Is G a virtually soluble group?

A group is said to be self-similar if it admits a faithful state-closed representation by automorphisms of a regular one-rooted m-tree for some m. Can a torsion-free finitely presented metabelian group which is self-similar contain a subgroup isomorphic to the restricted wreath product H = Z ≀ Z? It is known that Z≀Z itself is self-similar(A. C. Dantas, T. M. G. Santos, S. N. Sidki, J. Algebra, 567(2021), 564–581).

Let Td,c denote the class of d-generated, torsion-free nilpotent groups having class c. It is known that Td,2-groups are self-similar for all d, that T2,3-groups are self-similar, and that there are T4,3-groups that are not self-similar(A. Berlatto, T. Santos, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16947). Are there T3,3-groups that are not self-similar?
Conjecture: Suppose that for a fixed positive integer k at least half of the elements of a finite group G have order k. Then G is solvable.

Let Wn = A5 ≀· · ·≀A5 be the n-times iterated permutational wreath product of A5 in its natural action(so Wn acts on 5n points), and let W = lim Wn be the inverse ←− limit(infinite iterated wreath product of A5). Does W contain a finitely generated dense subgroup of subexponential growth?
(Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group requiring more than two generators? Cf. 6.44 in Archive.
(Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group of finite cohomological dimension greater than 2?

(Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented group G such that G ≅ G × H for some non-trivial group H? The first finitely generated example was constructed in(J. M. Tyrer Jones, J. Austral. Math. Soc., 17(1974), 174–196). A finitely presented group that surjects onto its own direct square was constructed in(G. Baumslag, C. F. Miller, III, Bull. London Math. Soc., 20, no. 3(1988), 239–244).

A quasimorphism on a group G is a function f: G → R such that the quantity sup |f(g) + f(h) − f(gh)| is finite. A quasimorphism is homogeneous if it restricts to g,h a homomorphism on every cyclic subgroup of G. Let G be a group admitting an unbounded homogeneous quasimorphism G → R that is not a homomorphism. Must G contain a non-abelian free subgroup?

An isometric action of a group G on a metric space S is called acylindrical if for every ε > 0 there exist R, N > 0 such that for every two points x, y with d(x, y) ⩾ R, there are at most N elements g ∈ G satisfying d(x, gx) ⩽ ε and d(y, gy) ⩽ ε. A group is said to be acylindrically hyperbolic if it is not virtually cyclic and admits an acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space with unbounded orbits. Is the automorphism group of a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group also acylindrically hyperbolic?

Does every finite 3-group T have a nontrivial characteristic subgroup C such that if T is a Sylow 3-subgroup of a finite group G, then T ∩ G′ = T ∩ H ′, where H = NG(C)? Such a characteristic subgroup is known to exist in p-groups for p ⩾ 5(G. Glauberman, Math. Z., 117(1970), 46–56), and for p = 3 there are two characteristic subgroups K1, K2 such that T ∩ G′ = (T ∩ H1′)(S ∩ H2′), where Hi = NG(Ki) (G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 648(2024), 62–86). The group S4 shows that no such characteristic subgroups can be found in some Sylow 2-subgroups.

Let p be a prime, and P a finite p-group. (a) Suppose that P has an abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal abelian subgroup of order pn? (b) Suppose that P has an elementary abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order pn? It is easy to see that for p = 2, the answer to(b) is “yes” only for n = 1. The answer to both questions is “yes” for n < (p + 2)/2(G. G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 319, no. 2(2008), 800–805), as well as for n ⩽ 5 when p ̸= 2(M. Konvisser, D. Jonah, J. Algebra, 34(1975), 309–330). The answer to both questions is “no” for n ⩾ (p+9)/2 when p ⩾ 5(for p ⩾ 7 due to G. Glauberman, Contemp. Math., 524(2010), 61–65; for p = 3, 5 due to Ya. G. Berkovich, J. Algebra, 248, no. 2(2002), 472–553). Thus, the only open cases for p ⩾ 5 are n = 6 for p = 5, and n = (p + 3)/2, (p + 5)/2, (p + 7)/2 for p > 5.

Let L be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let D be a conjugacy class of involutions in L. Consider the complete graph Γ with vertex set D. Define an equivalence relation ∼ (graph coloring) on the set of edges as follows: (a, b) ∼ (c, d) if and only if |ab| = |cd|. An automorphism of the coloured graph Γ is a permutation τ ∈ SD such that(a, b) ∼ (aτ, bτ) for every edge(a, b). Is it true that the automorphism group of Γ is a subgroup of Aut(L)?

In the notation of 21.52, let Autt(Γ) be the set of permutations τT∈ SD such that(a, b) ∼ (aτ, bτ) whenever |ab| = t for a, b ∈ D. Clearly, Aut(Γ) = t Autt(Γ). Is it true that for every finite simple group G we have Aut(Γ) = Aut2(Γ) ∩ Autp(Γ), where {2, p} are the two minimal prime divisors of |G|?

Let G be a finite soluble group with triality, which means that G admits a group of automorphisms S isomorphic to the symmetric group of degree 3 given by the presentation S = ⟨σ, ρ | σ 2 = ρ3 = 1; σρσ = ρ2 ⟩ such that m · mρ · mρ = 1 for all m in the set of commutators M(G):= {[g, σ] | g ∈ G}. Suppose in addition that G = [G, S], the group G is generated by d elements of M(G) and their images under S, and xn = 1 for all x ∈ M(G). Is it true that the Fitting height of G is bounded in terms of d and n? An affirmative answer would provide a reduction of the analogue of the Restricted Burnside Problem for Moufang loops to the nilpotent case.
Let q be a power of a prime p, and let mn(q) be the maximum p-length of p-solvable subgroups of GL(n, q). Is it true that lim mn(q)/ log2 n = 1? İ. Güloğlu n→∞

Let ℓ(X) denote the composition length of a finite group X. Let A be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group G. Let c(G, A) be the number of trivial A-modules in a given A-composition series of G. (Note that c(G, A) = ℓ(CG(A)) if(|A|, |G|) = 1.) Conjecture: there are absolute constants C1 and C2 such that the Fitting height of G is at most C1 ℓ(A) + C2 c(G, A). İ. Güloǧlu

Let X be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. Let H be an X-maximal subgroup of a finite group G, and N a normal subgroup of G. Must H ∩ N be an X-maximal subgroup of N?

We say that a product XY = {xy | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y } of two subsets X, Y of a group G is direct if for every z ∈ XY there are unique x ∈ X, y ∈ Y such that z = xy. Is there an infinite group G such that every subset A ⊆ G satisfies the following property: all the maximal subsets B for which the product AB is direct have the same cardinality? Note that for checking the property for a given infinite group G, it suffices to consider only those subsets A ⊆ G for which |A| = |G \ A|. Indeed, the property is equivalent to A−1 A ∩ BB −1 = {1} and A−1 AB = G, and these imply |G| = |A||B|, since G is infinite. Now, if |A| < |G \ A|, then |A| < |G|, and so |B| = |G|; and if |A| > |G \ A|, then A−1 A = G, and so |B| = 1, for all B satisfying the property.

For a finite group G, let χ1(G) denote the totality of the degrees of all irreducible complex characters of G with allowance for their multiplicities. Suppose that H is a finite group with χ1(H) = χ1(G). a) If G is an almost simple group, must H be isomorphic to G? b) If G is a quasisimple group, must H be isomorphic to G? This is true if G is a simple group(see 11.8(a) in Archive).

Let G be a finite group, Z(p) the localization at p, and Fp the field of p elements. Let X be the class of Fp G-modules obtained by reduction of simple QG-modules. Is it true that Z(p) G is semiperfect if and only if each projective indecomposable Fp G-module can be written as an N-linear combination of modules in X inside the Grothendieck group of Fp G? The “only if” direction is proved, and the affirmative answer is obtained if p does not divide |G| (D. Johnston, D. Rumynin, J. Algebra, 687, no. 1(2026), 776–791).
For a fixed(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given a finite subset S of G, finds a finite presentation for the subgroup H = ⟨S⟩? Cf. 4.8 in Archive.

Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic groups? That is, for a fixed group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given elements w, h1,..., hk ∈ G, decides whether or not w belongs to the subgroup H = ⟨h1,..., hk ⟩?

(E. Zelmanov). Let F be a field of characteristic p > 0, and let Γ be the principal congruence subgroup of Aut(F [x1,..., xn ]) consisting of all automorphisms that send each variable xi to xi modulo terms of higher degree. Then Γ is a residuallyp group. Does Γ satisfy a pro-p identity?
Is it true that if a normal subgroup A of a Sylow p-subgroup of a p-soluble finite group G has exponent pe, then the normal closure of A in G has(p, e)-bounded(or even e-bounded) p-length?

Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G. Must G contain a subgroup of index bounded in terms of |φ| and |CG(φ)| whose Fitting height is bounded(a) in terms of |φ|? (b) or even in terms of the composition length of ⟨φ⟩? An affirmative answer to part(b) is known when |φ| is a prime power(B. Hartley– V. Turau), or when(|G|, |φ|) = 1(A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs). Also cf. 19.43.

Suppose that A is a nilpotent group of automorphisms of a finite soluble group G. Is the Fitting height of G bounded in terms of |A| and |CG(A)|? An affirmative answer is known when(|G|, |A|) = 1(J. G. Thompson, even for soluble A, with improved bounds in subsequent papers of H. Kurzweil, A. Turull, B. Hartley–I. M. Isaacs), when A is cyclic(see 19.43), or when CG(A) = 1(E. C. Dade). Note that for any non-nilpotent finite group A there are finite soluble groups G of unbounded Fitting height with CG(A) = 1(S. D. Bell–B. Hartley).

Suppose that φ is an automorphism of a finite soluble group G, and let r be the(Prüfer) rank of the fixed-point subgroup CG(φ). Is the Fitting height of G bounded terms of |φ| and r? This is known to be true in the case where |φ| is a product of at most two prime powers(B. Hartley, Preprint, 1994, https://kourovkanotebookorg.wordpress. com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/hartley94-prepr-mims.pdf). An affirmative answer to this question would imply an affirmative answer to 13.8(b).

A finite group G is said to be semi-abelian if it has a sequence of subgroups 1 = G0 ⩽ G1 ⩽ · · · ⩽ Gn = G such that for every i the subgroup Gi+1 is isomorphic to a quotient of a semidirect product Ai ⋊ Gi for some abelian group Ai. Conjecture: Semi-abelian finite groups are monomial.
Is there an algorithm deciding if a given one-relator group is hyperbolic?

A group G is called an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n over a ring R if it is of type FP over R and Hi(G; RG) = 0 for i ̸= n, while Hn(G; RG) = R as an RG-module, where the action on R is trivial. (Note that G is not required to be finitely presented.) If G is an orientable Poincaré duality group of dimension n over all fields, is it an orientable Poincaré duality group over the integers?

For a ring R, we say that a group G is of type FL(R) if the trivial RG-module R admits a finite resolution by finitely generated free modules. If R is a field, we define the Euler characteristic of G over R to be the alternating sum of R-ranks of homology groups Hi(G; R). Does there exist a group of type FL(Fi) for two fields F1 and F2 such that the Euler characteristics of the group over the fields F1 and F2 differ?

We say that a group is a Tarski monster if it is finitely generated, not cyclic, and all of its proper non-trivial subgroups are isomorphic to each other. a) Do there exist amenable torsion-free Tarski monsters? b) Do there exist amenable Tarski monsters of prime exponent?
Is the conjugacy problem in CT(Z) algorithmically decidable? See the definition of CT(Z) in 17.57.
Is it algorithmically decidable whether a given element g ∈ CT(Z) (a) permutes a nontrivial partition of Z into residue classes? (b) has only finite cycles? (c) has no finite cycles?
Given two distinct sets P1 and P2 of odd primes none of which is a subset of the other, is it true that ⟨CTP1(Z), CTP2(Z)⟩ ⪇ CTP1 ∪P2(Z)? See the definition of CTP(Z) in 17.60.

Let σ = (σij), 1 ⩽ i ̸= j ⩽ n, be an irreducible elementary net(carpet) of order n ⩾ 3 over a field K(see 19.48). The net σ is said to be closed if the elementary net subgroup E(σ) does not contain new elementary transvections. The net σ is said to be completable if its diagonal can be supplemented with subgroups to a complete net. Completable elementary nets are closed. It is known that over fields of characteristic 0 and 2 there exist irreducible closed elementary nets that are not completable(V. A. Koibaev, Trudy Inst. Mat. Mekh. Ural Div. Ross. Akad. Nauk, 17, no. 4(2011), 134–141(Russian); V. A. Koibaev, Siberian Math. J., 62, no. 2(2021), 262–266). Do there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order n ⩾ 3 over a field of odd characteristic that are not completable?

Let d be an integer that is not divisible√by n-th powers of primes, let xn − d be an irreducible polynomial over Q, let θ = n d, and let K = Q(θ) be the radical extension of degree n of the field Q. The multiplicative group K ∗ of the field K is canonically embedded into the group AutQ(K) of all invertible Q-linear mappings of the Q-space K; let T be the image of K ∗ under this embedding. In the natural basis 1, θ, θ2,..., θn−1 of the Q-space K the group AutQ(K) corresponds to G = GL(n, Q), and the subgroup T to a subgroup T(d) (unsplit maximal torus). Every subgroup H of G containing T(d) and some one-dimensional transformation is rich in elementary transvections(V. A. Koibaev, St. Petersbg. Math. J., 21, no. 5(2010), 731–742) and thus defines a net σ = σ(H) (V. A. Koibaev, A. V. Shilov, J. Math. Sci. New York 171, no. 3(2010), 380–385). Let E(σ) denote the subgroup generated by all transvections in the net group G(σ). Is it true that H ⩽ NG(E(σ))? This inclusion was proved in the case n = 2(V. A. Koibaev, Dokl. Math., 41, no. 3(1990), 414–416).

Let p be a prime and let G be a pro-p group. Suppose that all of the(continuous Galois) cohomology groups H n(G, Fp) of G with coefficients in the field of p elements are finite. Does it necessarily follow that the cohomology ring H ∗ (G, Fp) is finitely generated? The answer is known to be ‘yes’ if G is abelian-by-(p-adic analytic), as follows from(J. King, Commun. Algebra, 27, no. 10(1999), 4969–4991).

Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S and the corresponding word metric LS(∗). An element g is said to be distorted in G if LS(g n)/n → 0 as n → ∞; this notion is independent of the choice of the generating set S. For any, not necessarily finitely generated, group H, an element g ∈ H is said to be distorted if there is a finitely generated subgroup G of H containing g in which g is distorted. Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups in which every nontrivial element is distorted? Note that it is straightforward to construct countable(not finitely generated) left-orderable groups with this property using HN N-extensions and applying results of V. V. Bludov and A. M. W. Glass.

Do there exist finitely generated left-orderable groups with only one nontrivial conjugacy class? A positive answer to this question implies a positive answer to 21.78. Note that D. Osin constructed torsion-free finitely generated groups with only one nontrivial conjugacy class; see 9.10 in Archive.

(J. Wiegold). Let Γ be a finite simple group and let Nn(Γ) denote the set of normal subgroups of the free group Fn of rank n whose quotient is isomorphic to Γ. Conjecture: Aut(Fn) acts transitively on Nn(Γ) for n ⩾ 3. This is not true for n = 2(B. H. Neumann, H. Neumann, Math. Nachr., 4(1951), 106–125).

Conjecture: For n ⩾ 3, there are no finite simple characteristic quotients of the free group Fn. This is not true for n = 2(W. Y. Chen, A. Lubotzky, P. H. Tiep, to appear in Comment. Math. Helvetici, 2025).

The function dn(σ, τ) = (1/n)·|{x ∈ {1,..., n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| is a distance on the symmetric group Sn. For a finitely generated group G, an almost-homomorphism is a sequence of set-theoretic maps fn: G → Sn satisfying dn(fn(g)fn(h), fn(gh)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g, h ∈ G. An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn: G → Sn such that dn(ρn(g), fn(g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is close to a homomorphism. Conjecture: Metabelian groups are permutation-stable.

For σ ∈ Sn and τ ∈ Sm, where n ⩽ m, let dflex n(σ, τ) = (1/n) · (|{x ∈ {1,..., n} | σ(x) ̸= τ (x)}| + (m − n)). An almost-homomorphism {fn } is said to be flexibly close to a homomorphism if there is a sequence of group homomorphisms ρn: G → Smn with n ⩽ mn such that dflex n(ρn(g), fn(g)) → 0 as n → ∞ for all g ∈ G. The group G is said to be flexibly permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of G is flexibly close to a homomorphism. Is SLn(Z) flexibly permutation-stable?
Is a flexibly permutation-stable group always permutation-stable?

(M. Gromov, B. Weiss). A group G is said to be sofic if for every finite set F ⊆ G containing 1 and every ε > 0 there exist n ∈ N and a map φ: F → Sn such that φ(1) = 1, d(φ(gh), φ(g)φ(h)) < ε for all g, h such that gh ∈ F, φ(g) does not have fixed points for every g ∈ F \ {1}. Is every group sofic?

Assume that a finite group G has a family of d-generator subgroups whose indices have no common divisor. Is it true that G can be generated by d + 1 elements? The answer is positive if G is solvable(L. G. Kovács, H.-S. Sim, Indag. Math., 2(1991), 229–232). For an arbitrary finite group G it is proved that G can be generated by d + 2 elements(A. Lucchini, Commun. Algebra, 28, no. 4(2000), 1875–1880).
Is there a finite non-abelian group G of odd order, with k(G) conjugacy classes, such that k(G)/|G| = 1/17?

For n > 39, is it true that the number of conjugacy classes in the symmetric group Sn of degree n is never a divisor of the order of Sn? In other words, is it true that, for n > 39, the number p(n) of integer partitions of n is never a divisor of n!?

Let Γ be a graph of diameter d. For i ∈ {1, 2,..., d}, let Γi be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ with vertices u, w adjacent in Γi if and only if dΓ (u, w) = i. Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that Γ2 and Γ3 are strongly regular? A. A. Makhnëv

(W. Willems). Conjecture: The sum of squares of the degrees of the irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is at least the p′-part of |G|. This is known to be true for p = 2(G. Malle, Adv. Math., 380(2021), Paper no. 107609, 15 pp.).
Conjecture: The number of irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is bounded above by the maximum of the number of conjugacy classes k(H) in p′-subgroups H of

(M. Herzog, J. Schönheim). Let G be a group and let k ⩾ 2. Let H1,..., Hk be subgroups of G, and g1,..., gk elements of G such that the cosets g1 H1,..., gk Hk form a partition of G. Is it true that |G: Hi | = |G: Hj | for some i ̸= j? This is known to be true for groups with a Sylow tower(M. A. Berger, A. Felzenbaum, A. Fraenkel, Fund. Math., 128, no. 3(1987), 139–144). Also cf. 20.99.

The Gruenberg–Kegel graph(or the prime graph) GK(G) of a finite group G is a labelled graph with vertex set consisting of all prime divisors of the order of G in which different vertices p and q are adjacent if and only if G contains an element of order pq. Let GK(G) denote the abstract graph obtained from GK(G) by removing all labels. A finite group G is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there are no finite groups H not isomorphic to G with GK(H) isomorphic to GK(G). Are there infinitely many(pairwise non-isomorphic) finite groups which are recognizable by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph?

Is there an almost simple but not simple group which is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph? Note that if a group G is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg– Kegel graph, then G is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and therefore G is almost simple(P. J. Cameron, N. V. Maslova, J. Algebra, 607(2022), 186–213).
Is it true that a periodic group containing an involution is locally finite if the centralizer of every element of even order is locally finite?

(M. Tărnăuceanu). Is it true that for every positive rational number r there exists a finite group G such that | Aut(G)|/|G| = r? A similar question is answered in the positive for graphs, monoids, partial groups, and posets(R. Molinier, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21059). It is also known that the set {| Aut(G)|/|G| | G is a finite abelian group} is dense in [0, +∞) (M. Tărnăuceanu, Elemente Math. (2025), https://ems.press/journals/ em/articles/14298544).

Let w be a multilinear commutator word, and assume that G is a group where the set of w-values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups. Is it true that the verbal subgroup w(G) is finite-by-cyclic? This is true for lower central words(G. Cutolo, C. Nicotera, J. Algebra, 324, no. 7(2010), 1616–1624).

Conjecture: If G is a transitive permutation group on a finite set Ω, then for any distinct α, β in Ω there is an element g ∈ G with αg = β whose number of fixed points is different from 1. P. Müller

Suppose that A and G are finite groups such that A acts coprimely on G by automorphisms. Let C = CG(A) be the fixed-point subgroup, and let C ′ denote its derived subgroup. Is it true that the number of A-invariant irreducible characters χ of G whose restriction χC is never zero is exactly |C/C ′ |? This would follow if one could show that χC is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent χ∗ of χ is linear.

Which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of regular polytopes of rank 3? In other words, which finite almost simple groups are generated by three involutions two of which commute? This question has been answered for finite simple groups; see 7.30 in Archive. Ya.

Let V be a variety generated by a finite group, and let f(n)p be the order of the free group in V on n generators. Is it true that the sequence n log f(n) has a limit as n → ∞, and this limit is an integer?

(V. V. Uspenskii). A Hausdorff topological group G is called minimal if it does not admit a strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is called Raikov complete if its two-sided uniform structure is complete. It is known that a finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again minimal. Is it true that an arbitrary Cartesian product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups remains minimal? It is known that an arbitrary Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological groups is minimal(M. Megrelishvili, Topology Appl., 62, no. 1(1995), 1–19).

For a group word w(x1,..., xn) on n letters, define e0(x1,..., xn) = x1 and ek+1(x1,..., xn) = w(ek(x1,..., xn),..., xn) for all k ∈ N. A group G is said to satisfy the Engel type iterated identity w if for all x1,..., xn ∈ G there exists m ∈ N such that em(x1,..., xn) = 1. Conjecture: For every non-trivial word w, if a finitely generated branch group G(see 15.12) satisfies the iterated identity w, then G is a torsion group. This is true in the case of the commutator word w = [x1, x2 ] (G. Fernández- Alcober, M. Noce, G. Tracey, J. Algebra, 554(2020), 54–77).

(D. Segal). A group word w is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gw of word values of w in G is finite, the verbal subgroup w(G) = ⟨Gw ⟩ is also finite(see also Archive 2.45). Is every word concise in the class of residually finite groups? See(D. Segal, Words. Notes on verbal width in groups, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2009) for a partial solution.

A first order formula φ(x) in the group language with one free variable is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gφ of elements in G satisfying φ is finite, the subgroup φ(G) generated by Gφ is also finite(cf. 21.105 and Archive 2.45). Is every formula with one free variable concise in the class of residually finite groups?

A sequence {Fn } of pairwise disjoint finite subsets of a topological group is called expansive if for every open subset U there is a number m such that Fn ∩ U ̸= ∅ for all n > m. Suppose that a countable group G can be partitioned into countably many dense subsets. Is it true that in G there exists an expansive sequence? Cf. 15.80.

For a finite group G let Cod(G) denote the set of irreducible character codegrees of G(see 20.78). Define σ(G) = max{|π(m)|: m ∈ Cod(G)}, where π(m) denotes the set of prime divisors of an integer m. It is proved that there exists a constant k such that |π(G)| ⩽ k · σ(G) for every finite group G(Y. Yang, G. Qian, J. Algebra, 478(2017), 215–219), but the estimate provided for k is very crude. Can the constant k be taken as 4?

Conjecture: The derived length of a finite solvable group G does not exceed |Cod(G)| − 1. The Fitting height of G is known to be at most min{|Cod(G)|−1, |Cod(G)|/2+1} (G. Qian, Y. Zeng, J. Group Theory, to appear).

Let S be a nonabelian finite simple group, and x a nonidentity automorphism of S. Let α(x) be the smallest number of conjugates of x in G = ⟨x, Inn S⟩ that generate G. The values of α(x) had been studied in(R. Guralnick, J. Saxl, J. Algebra, 268, no. 2(2003), 519–571). (a) (R. Guralnick, J. Saxl). Conjecture: If S is an exceptional group of Lie type, then α(x) ⩽ 5 for every nonidentity automorphism x of S. (b) For each exceptional group S of Lie type, find the largest value of α(x).

Let S be a finite simple nonabelian group that is not isomorphic to any group 2B2(q). A nonidentity automorphism x of S is called a τ-automorphism if every two conjugates of x in ⟨x, Inn(S)⟩ generate a subgroup of order not divisible by 3. If S admits a τ-automorphism, we call S a τ-group. (a) List all τ-groups up to isomorphism. (b) Do τ-automorphisms of odd order exist?

A nonempty class X of finite groups is said to be complete if X is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of a complete class X other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest integer n such that Sn ∈ X. Every positive integer n ̸= 3 coincides with the symmetric boundary of some complete class. It is proved(mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i Analiz, 37, no. 1(2025), 141–176(Russian)) that, for every complete class X, there exists a nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group G and each conjugacy class D of G, if every m elements of D generate a subgroup belonging to X, then ⟨D⟩ ∈ X. The smallest such m is called the Baer–Suzuki width of X denoted by BS(X). It is also proved(mod CFSG, ibid.) that, for a complete class X of symmetric boundary n, the value of BS(X) is at least n and is bounded above in terms of n. For every positive integer n ̸= 3, let f+ (n) and f− (n) be respectively the maximum and the minimum of BS(X), where X runs over all complete classes of symmetric boundary n. (a) Find f+ (n) for n = 4, 5, 6. It is known that f+ (1) = 2, f+ (2) = 3, and f+ (n) = 2(n − 1) for n ⩾ 7. (b) Is it true that f− (n) = n for all n ̸= 3? This is known to be true for n = 1, 2, 4.

Let G be a finite group and p be a prime. Let Ψp,G be the class function of G which vanishes on all p-singular elements of G and whose value at each p-regular element x of G is the number of p-elements of CG(x). (a) Is it true that Ψp,G is a character of G? (b) If yes, can Ψp,G be afforded by a projective RG-module, where R is a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero such that the field of fractions of R is a splitting field for G and its subgroups, and the residue field R/J(R) is a splitting field of characteristic p for G and its subgroups? It is known that Ψp,G is a character when G ≅ Sn for any positive integer n and any prime p(T. Scharf, J. Algebra, 139, no. 2(1991), 446–457).

A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H: [H, H]| ⩽ |G: [G, G]| for all H ⩽ G. Do weakly ab-maximal groups have bounded derived length? It is known that weakly ab-maximal groups are direct products of weakly abmaximal p-groups(F. Lisi, L. Sabatini, J. Group Theory, 27(2024), 1203–1217).

Let C1,..., Cn be(left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U:= C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n? Affirmative answers are known in some special cases(B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu, J. Algebraic Combin., 55(2022), 979–987).
A group is boundedly acyclic if its bounded cohomology with trivial real coefficients vanishes in all positive degrees. Is every branch group boundedly acyclic?

(a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth? (b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth?
(A. Thom). Is there any group which is not isomorphic to the quotient of a residually finite group by an amenable normal subgroup?
Does there exist a group G that contains a family(Gn)n∈N of finite-index subgroups such that for every n there is a homomorphism fn: Gn → Z whose kernel is of type Fn, but not of type Fn+1?

A pro-p group is(relatively) strictly finitely presented if it is the pro-p completion of a group that is finitely presented(respectively, finitely presented in some finitely-based variety of groups). A pro-p group is finitely axiomatizable if it is determined up to isomorphism by a single sentence in the first-order language of group theory. (a) Does there exist a(relatively) strictly finitely presented pro-p group that is not finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups? (b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable? See(A. Nies, K. Tent, D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3), 123(2021), 597– 635; D. Segal, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04816).

Let p be a prime number. A group Γ is called p-Jordan if there exist constants J and e such that any finite subgroup G ⊂ Γ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order coprime to p and of index at most J · |G(p) |e. (For example by the results of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field K of characteristic p the group GLn(K) is p-Jordan with e = 3.) Let the p-Jordan exponent e(Γ) of the group Γ be the infimum of all constants e for which the above bound holds for some constant J = J(e). a) Is it true that this infimum is always attained? b) Is it true that e(Γ) ⩽ 3 for any p-Jordan group Γ?

Let w be a group word, and G a profinite group. Is it true that the cardinality of the set of w-values in G is either finite or at least continuum? An affirmative answer is known for several important words; see(E. Detomi, B. Klopsch, P. Shumyatsky, J. London Math. Soc. (2), 102(2020), 977–993).

Is it true that the extension of the A. Agrachev–R. Gamkrelidze construction of groups from pre-Lie rings in(J. Soviet Math., 17(1981), 1650–1675) suggested in Definition 66 of(A. Smoktunowicz, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 229, no. 12(2025), 108128) produces groups from pre-Lie rings? If this extended construction does give a group, then it also gives a brace, and so an affirmative answer to this question would have consequences for the theory of set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and for the theory of braces.

A group G is said to be virtually special if G has a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a special complex(in the sense of F. Haglund, D. T. Wise, Geom. Funct. Anal., 17, no. 5(2008), 1551–1620; cf 20.60.) A group G is called a CAT(0) group if it acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly by isometries on a CAT(0) metric space. a) Is every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually special? b) A weaker question: does every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually embed into a right-angled Artin group?

(M. Bridson). Let Fm be a free group of rank m and let ϕ ∈ Aut(Fm) be a polynomially growing automorphism of maximal degree m − 1, which means that for some(equivalently, any) free basis {x1,..., xm } of Fm, the sequence maxi |ϕn(xi)| grows at the rate of nm−1, where |g| denotes the minimal length of g in the xi and their inverses. a) Is the free-by-cyclic group Fm ⋊ϕ Z virtually special? b) In particular, are the Hydra groups Gm = Fm ⋊ Z = ⟨a1,..., am, t | t−1 a1 t = a1, t−1 ai t = ai ai−1 for all i > 1⟩ virtually special?

(N. Brady). Do there exist finitely presented subgroups of right-angled Artin groups whose Dehn functions are super-exponential, or sub-exponential but not polynomial? Such subgroups are known to exist in general CAT(0) groups, whereas the only Dehn functions currently realized for subgroups of right-angled Artin groups are exponential and polynomial of arbitrary degree.

Let G be a right-angled Artin group. Is the stable commutator length scl(g) a rational number for every g ∈ [G, G]? For free groups this is true by Calegari’s Rationality Theorem. (See 18.40 for the definition of scl(g).)

Two groups G1 and G2 are said to be commensurable if there exist finiteindex subgroups H1 ⩽ G1 and H2 ⩽ G2(not necessarily of the same index) such that H1 ∼= H2. Let A[F4 ] and A[H4 ] denote the Artin groups of spherical types F4 and H4, respectively. Are these two groups commensurable? This is the most difficult case in the classification of Artin groups of spherical type up to commensurability.
If two Artin groups of spherical type are quasi-isometric, must they be commensurable? (This is not true for right-angled Artin groups.)

Conjecture: Let G be a finite additive abelian group with |G| odd. Then any subset A of G with |A| = n > 2 can be written as {a1,..., an } in such a way that all the sums a1 + a2, a2 + a3,..., an−1 + an, an + a1 are distinct.
Construct a homomorphism of a subgroup of a Golod group(see 9.76) onto an infinite AT-group as defined in(A. V. Rozhkov, Math. Notes, 40, no. 5(1986), 827–836). Cf. 13.55

Based on the development of E. S. Golod’s construction(see, for example, Discrete Math. Appl., 23, no. 5–6(2013), 491–501), for each prime number p, construct a finitely generated residually finite p-group with a non-trivial finite centre. Such groups with infinite and trivial centres are known(see 9.76 and Archive 11.101).
Does a group need to have a subnormal abelian series if every countable subgroup of it has such a series?

For a finite group G, let the type of G be the function on positive integers whose value at n is the number of solutions of the equation xn = 1 in G. a) Is it true that a group having the same type as a group with trivial solvable radical must also have trivial solvable radical? Note that there are solvable and nonsolvable groups with the same type(see 12.37). b) Is it true that a group having the same type as an almost simple group must be isomorphic to it? This is true for a group having the same type as a simple group, as follows from the affirmative answer to 12.39(in Archive).

For a finite group G, let χ1(G) denote the totality of the degrees of all irreducible complex characters of G with allowance for their multiplicities. Suppose that H is a finite group with χ1(H) = χ1(G). If G has trivial solvable radical, must H also have trivial solvable radical?

Let G be a profinite group with fewer than 2ℵ0 conjugacy classes of elements of infinite order. Must G be a torsion group? This holds in the case when G is finitely generated(J. S. Wilson, Arch. Math., 120(2023), 557–563). John

If the p-th powers in a finite p-group form a subgroup, must that subgroup be powerful? That is, for p ̸= 2, if the p-th powers in a p-group of exponent p2 form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian? For a 2-group of exponent 8, if the squares form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian?
Let G be an infinite finitely presented group such that every subgroup of infinite index is free. Must G be isomorphic to either a free group or a surface group?

Let G be a hyperbolic group which is virtually compact special in the sense of Haglund–Wise. Suppose that the set of second Betti numbers of the finite-index subgroups of G is bounded. Must G be virtually either a free group or a surface group?
Let G be a torsion-free group of type F∞ of infinite cohomological dimension. Must G contain a copy of Thompson’s group F?

Let G = G1*_H G2 be a free pro-p product of coherent pro-p groups with polycyclic amalgamation. Is G coherent? For abstract groups this is known to be true. A group is said to be coherent if each of its finitely generated subgroups is finitely presented, and in the question coherency is used in the pro-p sense.

A group G is said to be invariably generated by a and b if G is generated by the conjugates ag, bh for every g, h. Let p ̸= q be fixed primes. Does every finite group embed into a finite group invariably generated by an element of order p and an element of order q?
(Well-known problem). Is Thompson’s group F automatic?
(M. Brin, M. Sapir). Conjecture: Every subgroup of Thompson’s group F is either elementary amenable or else contains a subgroup isomorphic to F.
(M. Bridson). Is Thompson’s group F quasi-isometric(a) to F × Z? (b) to F × F?

(Well-known problem). A classifying space for a group G is a connected CW complex with fundamental group G and all higher homotopy groups trivial. A group is of type Fn if it has a classifying space with finite n-skeleton. For example, type F1 is equivalent to finite generation, and type F2 is equivalent to finite presentability. Type F∞ means type Fn for all n. For n ⩾ 3, does every group of type Fn−1 embed as a subgroup of a group of type Fn? Or even in a group of type F∞?

(V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). A subgroup H of a right-orderable group G is said to be right-relatively convex if it is convex under some right ordering on G. Is the lattice of right-relatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group always a sublattice of the lattice of its subgroups?
(V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Is it true that the lattice of rightrelatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group is distributive if and only if it is a chain?
(V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Are there order automorphisms of Dlab groups that are not inner automorphisms?

Let G be an extension of a normal elementary abelian subgroup A by an elementary abelian group B ≅ G/A such that A contains an element a with C_B(a) = 1. Is it true that the rank of the subgroup Z(⟨a, B⟩) ∩ (⟨a, B⟩)′ is at most the rank of B?

Let M be a connected Riemannian manifold isometrically immersed in Euclidean (n+1)-space E^(n+1). The immersion is of finite type when its position vector can be written as a finite sum x = c + x1 + ... + xk of E^(n+1)-valued Laplace eigenmaps satisfying Delta xi = lambda_i xi. Classify all finite type hypersurfaces in E^(n+1); in particular, classify all finite type surfaces in E^3.

Among compact surfaces immersed in Euclidean 3-space E^3, are the ordinary spheres the only compact surfaces whose immersion is of finite type, meaning that the position vector splits into finitely many Laplace eigensections?
context_brief: Compact finite type surfaces in E^3

question_text: In Euclidean 3-space E^3, are the only finite type surfaces minimal surfaces together with open portions of spheres and circular cylinders?
Among compact hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, are the only finite type examples the ordinary hyperspheres?

A hypersurface immersion is of 2-type when it is of finite type with exactly two distinct Laplace eigenvalues in its spectral decomposition. Study and classify 2-type hypersurfaces in a hypersphere of E^(n+2); in particular, classify 2-type hypersurfaces of S^4 in E^5.
Classify finite type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere in E^(n+2). Here finite type means that the position vector of the immersed hypersurface is a finite sum of Laplace eigenmaps.
Inside the unit 3-sphere S^3 subset E^4, are the only finite type surfaces the minimal surfaces, the standard 2-spheres, and the products of two plane circles?

A hypersurface M of S^(n+1) is called a Dupin hypersurface when the multiplicities of its principal curvatures are constant and each principal curvature is constant along its principal directions. Determine when such a Dupin hypersurface is of finite type, and determine when a finite type Dupin hypersurface of a hypersphere must be isoparametric.

Do there exist 2-type surfaces lying fully in S^4 whose immersion is not mass-symmetric, where mass-symmetric means that the center of gravity of the surface in E^5 coincides with the center of the ambient hypersphere?

Do there exist 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere of a Euclidean space? In particular, do there exist mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere?

Suppose a k-type immersion x : M -> E^m has spectral decomposition x = c + x1 + ... + xk, and for each i the subspace Ei is spanned by the values x_i(p) as p ranges over M. The immersion is called linearly independent when E1, ..., Ek are linearly independent. Study and classify linearly independent 2-type immersions.
Using the same notion of linearly independent immersion, study and classify linearly independent submanifolds of codimension 2.

A 2-type immersion is called null when one of its two Laplace eigenvalues is zero; equivalently, a non-null 2-type immersion has two nonzero eigenvalues. If an n-dimensional submanifold of Euclidean (n+2)-space is non-null 2-type and has constant mean curvature, must it be spherical?

A null 2-type submanifold is one whose mean curvature vector H satisfies Delta H = lambda H for some nonzero real constant lambda. Study and classify null 2-type submanifolds. In particular, classify all null 2-type surfaces in 4-dimensional Euclidean space and in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean spaces.

An isometric immersion x : M -> E^m is biharmonic when Delta^2 x = 0, equivalently Delta H = 0 for the mean curvature vector H. Other than minimal submanifolds, which submanifolds of Euclidean space E^m are biharmonic?
Are the only biharmonic submanifolds of Euclidean spaces the minimal ones?
Is every biharmonic hypersurface of a Euclidean space minimal?
Is every complete biharmonic submanifold of a Euclidean space minimal?

In recovery problems with noisy data, why do semidefinite-programming relaxations of maximum-likelihood estimators often remain tight beyond the exact-recovery regime? More concretely, when noise is large enough that the maximum-likelihood estimator cannot exactly recover the ground truth, under what structural or probabilistic conditions does the SDP relaxation still return a solution that lies in the original nonconvex model class, or equivalently matches the lower-rank quasi-maximum-likelihood solution instead of requiring a rounding step?

Let d > 1, n > 2, and m >= d + 1. Let A in R^(d x m) be a point cloud whose m columns are random points in R^d with i.i.d. uniform coordinates in [0,1]^d, and let O_1, ..., O_n be orthogonal transformations in R^d. Suppose the observed data are matrices A_i = O_i A + sigma eta_i in R^(d x m), where each eta_i has i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries. Form the generalized orthogonal Procrustes quasi-maximum-likelihood problem of maximizing Tr(CX) over block matrices X with X >= 0, X_ii = I_(d x d), and rank(X) <= d, and its semidefinite relaxation obtained by dropping the rank constraint. Does there exist a threshold sigma* > 0 such that whenever sigma < sigma*, with high probability the SDP relaxation has rank d and therefore exactly matches the quasi-maximum-likelihood solution?

For the modified focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation on R^d, with d = 2 in the no-group-velocity-dispersion case or d = 3 in the anomalous-group-velocity-dispersion case,

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0,

where f models high-intensity corrections such as a cubic-quintic or saturated nonlinearity, can one rigorously prove the oscillatory dynamics reported in experiments and numerics, in which a solution focuses, then defocuses, then refocuses, in an almost periodic or recurrent way rather than simply collapsing once?

Fix d in {2, 3}, let v_0 in H^1(R^d) be initial data for the cubic focusing NLS that produce a finite-time blow-up solution v at time T > 0, and let v_epsilon be the solution of the regularized equation

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0

with the same initial data. What is the limiting behavior of v_epsilon(t) as epsilon tends to 0 for times t > T, that is, after the blow-up time of the unregularized cubic NLS has already passed?

Consider the ionization-coupled variants of the focusing cubic NLS used for laser filamentation, namely the fixed-frame system

 i(partial_t + c_g partial_z)u + epsilon(Delta_perp + alpha_1 partial_z^2)u + epsilon(|u|^2 - rho)u = -i epsilon c(alpha_4 |u|^{2K-2}u + alpha_5 rho u),
 partial_t rho = epsilon alpha_4 |u|^{2K} + epsilon alpha_5 rho |u|^2,

and the moving-frame version

 i partial_tau v + (Delta_perp + alpha_1 partial_z^2)v + (|v|^2 - rho_tilde)v = -i c(alpha_4 |v|^{2K-2}v + alpha_5 rho_tilde v),
 -c_g partial_z rho_tilde = epsilon alpha_4 |v|^{2K} + epsilon alpha_5 rho_tilde |v|^2,

where the paper prescribes the boundary condition lim_{z -> +infinity} (nabla_perp)^l rho_tilde(tau, X_perp, z) = 0 for all l >= 0. Can one prove that solutions of these ionization models are global in dimensions 2 and 3, so that ionization really prevents finite-time collapse?

For the modified focusing cubic NLS

 i P_2(epsilon nabla) partial_t v + Delta v + |v|^2 v = 0,

assume that the positive self-adjoint operator P_2(epsilon nabla) gives only partial off-axis regularization, meaning it controls derivatives only in some distinguished directions rather than the full H^1 norm. Can one develop both the local and the global well-posedness theory in that partial off-axis case, and in particular decide whether this partial off-axis dependence is enough to prevent finite-time breakdown of solutions that would blow up for the standard focusing cubic NLS?

For the self-steepening model

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + i epsilon alpha_3 . nabla)(|v|^2 v) = 0

in dimension 2 for no group velocity dispersion or dimension 3 for anomalous group velocity dispersion, how can the finite-time blow-up solutions behave? In particular, can one rigorously describe the blow-up scenarios, including whether solutions can develop the shock-like profiles that the paper associates with optical self-steepening?

For the hyperbolic or non-elliptic cubic NLS

 i partial_t v + (Delta_perp - partial_z^2)v + |v|^2 v = 0

in dimensions 2 and 3, can one prove that every H^1 solution is global, despite the lack of the standard elliptic structure of the usual focusing cubic NLS?

For the hyperbolic cubic NLS

 i partial_t v + (Delta_perp - partial_z^2)v + |v|^2 v = 0,

can one rigorously prove and describe the pulse-splitting phenomenon seen in simulations, where a concentrating pulse reaches a threshold and then separates into lower-amplitude pulses moving apart instead of forming a singularity?

When partial off-axis variation of the group velocity and longitudinal self-steepening are both present in the same direction, namely for

 i(1 - epsilon^2 partial_z^2) partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + i epsilon partial_z)(|v|^2 v) = 0,

do solutions still exhibit self-steepening, or does the off-axis regularization suppress or qualitatively change that shock-like steepening effect?

For the two-component complex vector version of the modified NLS model, where v is C^2-valued and satisfies

 i P_2(epsilon nabla) partial_tau v + (Delta_perp + alpha_1 partial_z^2)v + i alpha_2 v + (1/3)(1 + i epsilon alpha_3 . nabla)((v . v)v + 2|v|^2 v) = 0,

can one investigate the vectorial counterparts of the scalar open problems studied in the paper, including the analogues of the questions about global existence versus blow-up, pulse splitting, self-steepening, mixed effects, and long-time approximation of the underlying Maxwell equations?

The paper rigorously derives several NLS-type asymptotic models from Maxwell's equations and justifies them on times of order T/epsilon only while the approximating NLS-type solution stays bounded, which in the standard focusing case means times strictly before the focusing time T_foc. Can one rigorously justify at least one of these derived NLS-type models on a time interval [0, T/epsilon] with T greater than or equal to the focusing time T_foc, so that the approximation remains valid in the regime where the different models begin to differ in a physically meaningful way?

In bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one define a form of compatible relaxation together with a convergence-rate estimate derived from the compatible-relaxation factor rho_cr so that, for a chosen interpolation strategy, the estimate accurately predicts the performance of the resulting two-grid method?
How can least-squares interpolation and the bootstrap setup used to compute test vectors be combined in a way that is simultaneously optimal and robust for defining algebraic multigrid interpolation?

For Hermitian positive definite problems, how should the compatible relaxation, algebraic distance, least-squares interpolation, test-vector generation, and related bootstrap algebraic multigrid components be integrated into a practical overall algorithm, validated on a carefully chosen and diverse collection of test problems including systems of partial differential equations, so that the method becomes a fast solver usable in practice?

For non-Hermitian problems treated with Galerkin-based algebraic multigrid, how can one correctly characterize the algebraically smooth error, or near-kernel components, that restriction and interpolation must approximate on coarse levels when small-singular-vector information can fail to describe that near kernel unless the matrix is normal?

For indefinite, non-elliptic problems such as Helmholtz and Schroedinger operators in higher dimensions, how can bootstrap algebraic multigrid be developed so that several locally orthogonal prolongation operators and the resulting multiple Galerkin coarse-grid operators are constructed efficiently, and to what extent can those techniques be extended into fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations?
Determine the exact asymptotic growth of D(n), where D(n) is the minimum number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by an n-point set in the plane.
Characterize the planar n-point sets P with D(P) = O(n/sqrt(log n)), meaning sets that span a near-optimal number of distinct distances up to the currently best known order of magnitude.
Prove or disprove that, for some sufficiently small epsilon > 0, every near-optimal planar n-point set contains at least Omega(n^epsilon) points on a single line.
Prove or disprove that for every near-optimal planar n-point set P and every epsilon > 0, every constant-degree algebraic curve contains at most O(n^(0.5+epsilon)) points of P.

Find the asymptotic value of Dcurve(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by n points lying on a constant-degree algebraic curve in the plane when the curve contains neither a line nor a circle.
Find the exact value of Dno3l(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set with no three collinear points.

Find the exact value of Dhat_conv(n), where Dhat_conv(n) is the largest number such that every set of n points in strict convex position contains a point whose distances to the other n-1 points realize at least Dhat_conv(n) distinct values.

Find the asymptotic value of Dgen(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in general position, meaning no three points are collinear and no four points are cocircular.
Find the asymptotic value of Dpara(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in general position that determines no parallelograms.
Find the asymptotic value of D_d(n), where D_d(n) is the minimum number of distinct distances that an n-point set in R^d can determine.
Find the asymptotic value of D3^o(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by n points constrained to lie on a sphere in R^3.
context_brief: Points on a sphere in R3

question_text: Find the asymptotic value of Do_d(n) for d >= 4, where Do_d(n) is the minimum number of distinct distances determined by n points on a hypersphere in R^d.
Find the asymptotic value of Dcurve^(d)(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by n points on a constant-degree curve in R^d that does not contain an algebraic helix.
Derive non-trivial lower or upper bounds for distinct distances determined by points constrained to algebraic varieties in R^d for dimensions d >= 3.
Find the asymptotic value of D(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined between two planar point sets of sizes m and n when only cross-set distances are counted.

Find the asymptotic value of Dlines(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances between m points on one line and n points on another planar line when the two lines are neither parallel nor orthogonal.

Find the asymptotic value of Dcurves(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances between m points on one constant-degree algebraic curve and n points on another when the curves avoid the exceptional cases of containing parallel lines, orthogonal lines, or concentric circles.
Find the asymptotic value of Dline(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances between a set of m points on a line and a set of n unrestricted points in the plane.
context_brief: One collinear set and one free set

question_text: Find the asymptotic value of Dline(m,n) under the extra assumption that every line parallel or orthogonal to the given line contains only O(1) points of the unrestricted set.

Find the asymptotic value of D(3,n) when the three distinguished points are not collinear, where D(3,n) asks for the minimum number of distances determined between those three points and another set of n points.
context_brief: Three noncollinear points versus n points

question_text: Derive non-trivial bounds for bipartite distinct-distance problems in R^d for d >= 3.
Find the asymptotic value of subset(n), the largest number such that every n-point set in the plane contains a subset of that size in which no positive distance occurs more than once.
context_brief: Largest distinct-distance subset in the plane

question_text: Find the asymptotic value of subset(L) when L is a sqrt(n) by sqrt(n) integer lattice, where subset(L) is the size of the largest subset of lattice points that spans each positive distance at most once.
context_brief: Distinct-distance subset in the planar lattice

question_text: Find the asymptotic value of subset(L_d) when L_d is the d-dimensional integer lattice n^(1/d) x ... x n^(1/d), where subset(L_d) is the size of the largest subset whose positive distances are all unique.

Find the asymptotic value of subset_d(n) for d >= 3, where subset_d(n) is the largest number such that every n-point set in R^d contains a subset of that size in which each positive distance occurs at most once.
Find the asymptotic value of subset'(n), the largest number such that every n-point planar set contains a subset of that size which spans no isosceles triangles.

Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,3,2), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every three points determine at least two distinct distances, equivalently a set with no equilateral triangles.

Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,3,3), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every three points determine three distinct distances, equivalently a set with no isosceles triangles, including degenerate collinear ones.

Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,4,3), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every four points determine at least three distinct distances, equivalently a set with no squares.

Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,4,4), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every four-point subset determines at least four distinct distances; equivalently, the set contains no rhombus, no rectangle, and no deltoid with one vertex equidistant from the other three.
Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,4,5), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every four-point subset determines at least five distinct distances.
Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,5,9), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every five-point subset determines at least nine distinct distances.
Find stronger general lower bounds for phi(n,k,l), the minimum number of distinct distances forced in an n-point planar set when every k-point subset determines at least l distinct distances.
Prove or disprove that if a planar n-point set P spans only O(n/sqrt(log n)) distinct distances, then the additive energy E(P) = |{(a,b,c,d) in P^4 : a+b = c+d}| must be large.
For a finite set A in R, determine the asymptotic size of the difference set A-A under the assumption that the Cartesian product A x A spans few distinct distances in the plane.
Find the asymptotic value of Dhat(n), the largest function such that every n-point planar set contains a point incident to at least Dhat(n) distinct distances to the other points.
Find the asymptotic value of DhatSigma(n), where DhatSigma(n) is the minimum, over all planar n-point sets P, of the sum over p in P of the number of distinct distances from p to the rest of P.
Find the asymptotic value of L(m,n), the minimum number of distinct point-to-line distances determined by a set of m points and a set of n lines in the plane.
Find the asymptotic value of vgen(n), the minimum number of distinct vectors spanned by an n-point planar set in general position, meaning no three points are collinear and no four are cocircular.

Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. Is it possible that the Minkowski sum of the quasi relative interiors, qri C + qri D, is a proper subset of the quasi relative interior of the Minkowski sum, qri(C + D)?

Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let A and B be convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi interior by qi E := {x in E | cone(E - x) = X}. Assuming qi B is nonempty, must the equality A + qi B = qi(A + B) always hold?

Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be nonempty convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. If qri C intersect qri D is nonempty, can the inclusion qri(C intersect D) subset qri C intersect qri D fail?

For subsets A of {0,1,...,r} that are more-sums-than-differences (MSTD), explicit infinite constructions were known with density about C/r^4 among all subsets of [0,r]. Can one construct a substantially denser explicit family of MSTD sets, and in particular can one obtain an explicit family that occupies a positive proportion of all subsets of [0,r]?

An MSTD subset of the integers has more pairwise sums than pairwise differences. Starting from the minimal 8-element integer example, one can build an MSTD subset of Z^2 by taking its product with a 2-point set. Can one instead construct an MSTD subset of Z^2 directly, without obtaining it from an MSTD subset of Z by such a lifting procedure?

Let A be a subset of Z_n. The order of A is the least h such that hA = Z_n but (h-1)A != Z_n. Which integers can occur as orders of bases in Z_n, especially in the regime where the order grows linearly with n?

Define g_0 = 0 and, greedily, let g_i be the least positive integer such that {g_0,...,g_i} has no solutions to 5w + 2x = 5y + 2z. Define a_0 = 0, define a_i by the recurrence given in the paper, and let A be the set of sums of distinct a_i. Is the greedy set G exactly {5x + y : x in A and 0 <= y <= 4}?

Suppose the first N terms of an increasing sequence already form an initial segment of a basis of order 2 for the nonnegative integers, meaning every sufficiently small nonnegative integer is a sum of two elements of the full basis. Must every such initial segment be extendable to a minimal basis, that is, a basis from which removing any one element destroys the basis property?

For the unrestricted partition generating function product over m >= 1 of (1 + x^m + x^(2m) + ...), can one choose signs in some of the factors so that, after expansion, every coefficient belongs to {0, -1, 1}?

Find a proof that the irrationality measure of zeta(2) is finite without using the prime number theorem. Such a proof would give a route to deriving infinitude-of-primes information from the Euler product for zeta(2) without appealing to the prime number theorem inside the irrationality argument itself.
Give an elementary proof that there are infinitely many primes p such that neither p-2 nor p+2 is prime; in other words, prove by elementary means that infinitely many primes are not twin primes.

Let C be a sparse sequence such as the squares, a fractional-power sequence, or values of a polynomial of degree at least 2. For fixed h >= 2, let D_h(C,N) be the minimum size of an h-basis A subset [N] whose h-fold sumset covers C(N), and let Gamma_h/C be the limit of |C(N)| / D_h(C,N)^h when that limit exists. Is Gamma_h/C equal to 0 whenever C is given by a polynomial of degree at least 2?

Let x_1,...,x_{n+r} be elements of a finite abelian group. Is it true that either 0 occurs as an n-term subsequence sum, or else the set of n-term subsequence sums has combinatorial dimension at least r+1 in the sense defined in the paper via Davenport's constant and zero-sum-free sequences?

Let mu(n) be the minimum size of a subset of [n] that is maximal subject to containing no 3-term arithmetic progression. Is it true that mu(4^t) = 2^t, and more generally does one always have mu(n) >= sqrt(n)?

Let K be a compact subset of R^2 that meets every residue class modulo Z^2, and let A = (K-K) intersect Z^2. Which finite generating sets of Z^2 can arise in this way? In particular, can one realize the axis-cross set {(0,0),(±1,0),(0,±1)}?

Classify the sequences of odd integers d_1,d_2,... for which the set B = {d_i 2^i : i >= 0} yields unique finite {0,1}-subset-sum representations of all integers in the de Bruijn signed-binary setting described in the paper. Equivalently, which odd sequences are 'okay' in that representation problem?

Let A be a set of nonnegative integers containing 0 such that each iterated sumset hA has asymptotic density 0, even though A subset 2A subset 3A subset ... is an increasing chain. Must any nontrivial structure nevertheless appear in this sequence of sumsets, and if so, what must happen?

Let B_N be a ball in SL(2,Z). How many quadruples gamma_1,gamma_2,gamma_3,gamma_4 in B_N satisfy gamma_1 + gamma_2 = gamma_3 + gamma_4? Beyond the trivial lower bound and easy N^5 upper bound described in the paper, obtain a genuinely nontrivial upper bound, ideally of order about N^(4+epsilon).

For a finite group G, can one always choose a generating set A so that the sequence of sphere sizes S(1), S(2), S(3), ... determined by word length with respect to A is unimodal? The paper notes that computations usually show unimodality but that a general theorem is unknown, even for nonabelian finite groups.

Characterize the sequences of nonnegative integers that can occur, eventually, as asymptotic representation functions r(A,n) counting the number of representations of n as a sum of two elements of a set A of nonnegative integers.

A subset B of the natural numbers is called an essential component if sigma(A+B) > sigma(A) whenever 0 < sigma(A) < 1, and it is extraordinary if the ratio sigma(A+B)/sigma(A) tends to infinity in the liminf sense as sigma(A) tends to 0. Is every essential component necessarily an extraordinary component?

Do there exist nontrivial pairs of maps L and R such that the rooted binary tree z -> (L(z), R(z)) lists every positive rational number exactly once, analogously to the classical Calkin-Wilf tree? More ambitiously, can one classify all such functional pairs?

Fix m >= 0 and let d = ceil(log_3 m). For n >= d, is the maximum number of affine lines contained in a set of m points in F_3^n always equal to the maximum number of lines achievable by m points already lying in F_3^d? Equivalently, when maximizing lines, is it always optimal to compress the configuration into the smallest possible ambient dimension?

For Zeckendorf-type decompositions and more general linear recurrence decompositions, determine how the theory changes when some integers have multiple representations or no representation at all, and derive formulas for gap distributions and the distribution of the largest gap in terms of the recurrence coefficients.

For H_n = {(x,y) in Z x Z : xy congruent to 1 mod n and 1 <= x,y <= n-1}, let v(n) be the number of vertices of the convex hull of H_n. Is v(n) forced to tend to infinity with n, and can one sharpen the lower-density estimate for the error term D(n) = v(n) - 2(tau(n-1)-1) on the set where D(n)=0?

Let S be a numerical semigroup of genus g, and let weff(S) count pairs (x,y) with x an irreducible element of S, y a gap of S, and 0 < x < y. Characterize the genus-g numerical semigroups having largest possible effective weight.

Does there exist a subset A of the natural numbers that is simultaneously more-sums-than-differences, meaning |A+A| > |A-A|, and more-products-than-ratios, meaning |A·A| > |A/A|? If such sets exist, can one produce explicit infinite families of them?

Let A be an R-sectorial operator on an L^p-space with p in (1, infinity). Must the sectorial angle omega(A) equal the R-sectorial angle omega_R(A)? The same question is asked under stronger semigroup assumptions: if -A generates an analytic C_0-semigroup, does the equality still hold when the semigroup is positive, contractive, or both positive and contractive?
context_brief: Angles of R-sectorial operators on L^p

question_text: Let A be a sectorial operator on a UMD-Banach lattice, and assume that -A generates a positive contractive C_0-semigroup. Must A then have a bounded H-infinity calculus, have bounded imaginary powers, or be R-analytic?
context_brief: Positive contractive semigroups on UMD-Banach lattices

question_text: Let A be a sectorial operator on an L^p-space with p in (1, infinity), and assume that -A generates a contractive C_0-semigroup. Must A then have a bounded H-infinity calculus, have bounded imaginary powers, or be R-analytic?

Let A be a sectorial operator on an L^p-space with p in (1, infinity), and assume that -A generates a positive C_0-semigroup. Must A then have a bounded H-infinity calculus, have bounded imaginary powers, or be R-analytic?

Find an analogue, in the borderline case omega_H-infinity(A) = pi/2, of the characterizations known below the critical angle. On Hilbert spaces, if -A generates a contractive analytic C_0-semigroup then A has a bounded H-infinity calculus with omega_H-infinity(A) = omega(A) < pi/2, and conversely operators with bounded H-infinity calculus of angle less than pi/2 are similar to generators of contractive analytic semigroups. On L^p-spaces, if -A generates a contractive positive analytic C_0-semigroup then A has a bounded H-infinity calculus with angle less than pi/2, and conversely such operators admit the structural model described in Theorem 2.11. What is the correct corresponding characterization when the H-infinity angle is exactly pi/2?

Characterize exactly which C_0-semigroups on L^p-spaces admit a loose dilation within the class of all L^p-spaces. Here a semigroup (T(t))_{t >= 0} has a loose dilation in a class X if there exist a space Y in X, bounded linear maps J: X -> Y and Q: Y -> X, and a bounded C_0-group (U(t))_{t in R} on Y such that T(t) = Q U(t) J for every t >= 0.
Does every C_0-semigroup of positive contractions on a UMD-Banach lattice admit either a strict dilation or a loose dilation in the class of all UMD-spaces?

Theorem 3.19 states that if a Banach space X admits an unconditional basis, then every negative generator of an analytic semigroup on X is R-sectorial if and only if X is isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Does the same equivalence remain true in either of the larger classes consisting of all Banach spaces that admit a Schauder basis, or all separable Banach spaces?

Is it true that for every sequence (z_n)_{n>=0} in the d-dimensional unit cube [0,1)^d there exists a constant c_d > 0 such that the discrepancy D_N of the first N points satisfies D_N >= c_d (log N)^d / N for infinitely many N?
context_brief: general lower-bound conjecture for sequence discrepancy

question_text: Does there exist an absolute constant A such that for every positive integer N one can choose an integer a that is relatively prime to N and whose continued-fraction expansion for a/N has all coefficients bounded above by A?

Does there exist an absolute constant B such that for every positive integer N one can choose an integer a relatively prime to N for which the sum of all continued-fraction coefficients of a/N is less than B log N?

Fix chi < 1. Is there a constant C'_chi > 0 such that for every N, at least chi N^d choices of (a_1, ..., a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N produce the d-dimensional lattice point set (({n a_1 / N}, ..., {n a_d / N}))_{n=0}^{N-1} whose discrepancy D_N is at least C'_chi (log N)^(d-1) log log N / N?
context_brief: average lower bounds for lattice-point discrepancies

question_text: For fixed integers d >= 1 and m >= 2 and a prime base q, does there exist a constant B_tilde(d,q) > 0 such that, for every delta with 0 < delta < 1, at least (1-delta)#M_d(m) of the d-tuples C = (C_1, ..., C_d) of m x m matrices over Z_q generate digital nets whose discrepancy D_N satisfies D_N >= delta B_tilde(d,q) (log N)^(d-1) log log N / N for infinitely many N?
context_brief: average lower bounds for digital-net discrepancies

question_text: Can one prove an average-type lower bound, analogous to Open Problem 2, for the discrepancy of digital nets generated by rational functions over finite fields?
context_brief: average lower bounds for rational-function digital nets

question_text: For suitable phi, can one find an asymptotic formula with a small error term R_chi(h) for the count N(h; a_1, ..., a_d) of integer vectors (n_1, ..., n_d) with -h <= n_i <= h and fractional part {n_1 a_1 / N + ... + n_d a_d / N} < phi(n_1, ..., n_d), uniformly in the sense that for every chi < 1 the formula holds for at least chi N^d choices of (a_1, ..., a_d) with 0 <= a_i < N?

For fixed positive integers d_1, ..., d_l with d_1 + ... + d_l = d and pairwise coprime bases q_1, ..., q_l, what are the smallest possible upper-bound function g(N) and the largest possible lower-bound function f(N) such that almost all Halton-Niederreiter sequences with d_i-dimensional components in base q_i satisfy D_N = O(g(N)) and D_N = Omega(f(N))?

For fixed d_1, ..., d_l with d_1 + ... + d_l = d and coprime bases q_1, ..., q_l, what are the optimal lower and upper metrical orders f(N) and g(N) for the discrepancy D_N of almost all finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences, with respect to a suitable measure, whose d_i-dimensional components are in base q_i?
context_brief: metrical order for finite-row Halton-Niederreiter sequences

question_text: What is the discrepancy order of concrete Halton-Kronecker sequences such as ((x_n, {n sqrt(2)}))_{n>=0}, where (x_n)_{n>=0} is the one-dimensional Halton sequence in base 2, i.e. the van der Corput sequence?
